paras: The threatened lynching of William Hardy took place at Baconton, Mitchell County, Georgia, on November 22, 1903, after Hardy, a Black man, shot a member of a posse sent to arrest him. Posse gunfire wounded Hardy, and officers moved him to the Albany jail as a mob organized to lynch him. The posse member, Raymond Mullins, the mayor's son, died the next day, and Hardy was tried within eight days and hanged at Camilla on December 22.

According to an Albany dispatch, Hardy had been beating his wife on the morning of Sunday, November 22, and she appealed to the officers for protection. The Baconton marshal, who was unarmed, went to Hardy's house to arrest him and was told he would not be taken unless killed. The marshal then called several men to help him and got a Winchester rifle.

Returning about 10 a.m., the party forced open the front door, and Hardy fired on the first man to enter, Raymond Mullins, shooting him through the abdomen. Hardy ran from the house under fire; one shot struck his leg and a bullet from the marshal's rifle passed through his shoulder before he was captured.

The dispatch said it soon became "evident that a mob was in process of organizing" and that Hardy would be lynched unless the authorities moved him. A telephone call brought Sheriff Edward from Albany by buggy, and four miles out he met the party holding Hardy and took him to the Albany jail that afternoon. A later report said Hardy had been moved to avoid "two mobs," and that Baconton officers believed he would have been lynched had he stayed near the scene.

Mullins died at 9 a.m. on November 23, while Hardy, who said he had been drunk and remembered nothing of the shooting, told reporters he expected to be hanged. A special term of Mitchell County Superior Court was called at Camilla on November 30, because, a Thomasville dispatch said, "strong sentiment against the negro demanded an early trial." The case took a few hours, and Hardy was found guilty and sentenced to hang on December 22.

Because the Camilla jail was "small and insecure," Sheriff Smith held Hardy in the Thomas county jail until the execution. He was hanged at Camilla on December 22 and, in the papers' words, "met death quietly." No report of an inquest into the shooting of Hardy, or of any action against those forming the mob, appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News led its November 23 front page with "Death From a Mob Narrowly Escaped by William Hardy, a Negro," and the New-York Tribune ran the same dispatch as "Negro Almost Lynched." Both stories came from Albany and gave only the officers' account, describing Mullins as "one of the most prominent young men in Mitchell county" and Hardy only as "a negro." Neither commented on the mob, treating its formation as a fact to be managed by removing the prisoner.

The Savannah paper followed the case through Mullins's death, the trial and the hanging, while the Atlanta Constitution carried the execution in a column of Georgia briefs. Northern papers such as the Waterbury Evening Democrat and the Bennington Evening Banner printed a one-sentence hanging brief headed "Met Death Penalty Quietly," naming the dead man "Reynolds Mullins." No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Hardy
bases: A posse's arrest attempt ended with the posse wounding William Hardy and a mob organizing to lynch him, which officers forestalled by removing him to Albany (A1, A3, A4); the lynching was threatened, not carried out, and Hardy was later legally hanged (A5, A6).

The Savannah Morning News and the New-York Tribune both carried the Albany dispatch on the shooting and the near-lynching (A1, A2), and the Savannah paper's follow-ups on Mullins's death, the trial and the hanging are echoed in the Atlanta Constitution and wire briefs (A3, A5, A6, A9), though all early detail traces to one Albany dispatch.

accounts.label: Albany wire dispatch (officers' version)
accounts.gist: Hardy, warned he would be arrested for beating his wife, said he would not be taken alive; when the posse forced the door he fired on the first man in, Mullins, then ran and was shot and captured; a mob formed and officers removed him to Albany.

accounts.label: Hardy's statement
accounts.gist: Hardy said he was drunk when the shooting happened and remembered nothing of it.

accounts.label: Baconton officers
accounts.gist: The officers believed Hardy would have been lynched had he been kept near the scene.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Death From a Mob Narrowly Escaped by William Hardy, a Negro,' praised Mullins as 'one of the most prominent young men in Mitchell county,' and presented the posse's account as fact without comment on the mob.
The New-York Tribune ran the dispatch as 'Negro Almost Lynched,' and Northern papers later carried a one-sentence hanging brief headed 'Met Death Penalty Quietly'.
Georgia papers reported the swift trial ('Strong sentiment against the negro demanded an early trial') and the hanging in brief items without comment.

conflicts.note: The Georgia reports consistently say Raymond; 'Reynolds' appears only in the Northern wire brief of the hanging and is likely a transmission error.
